title: Modern Machine Knitting:
author: Sue Jalowiec
excerpt: Yes, You Can Knit Contemporary Styles on Your Knitting Machine
body:
**Modern Machine Knitting:

Yes, You Can Knit Contemporary Styles on Your LK150**

Most knitters have seen it: machine-knitting patterns that look straight out of the 80s — oversized shoulders, stiff silhouettes, and design lines that don’t match the clean, modern shapes we love today.

A knitter wrote to me recently and said:

“I want to master my LK150. I want to make pieces as beautiful and contemporary as my hand-knitted ones — but most machine patterns look too 80s for my taste.”

If you’ve ever felt the same, this post is for you.

Because here’s the truth:

**Machine knitters aren’t limited to dated patterns.

You can knit modern, beautiful, contemporary garments — with confidence.**

And if you’re already a hand knitter?
You have a huge advantage.

Your hand-knitting experience is your superpower

Hand knitters come to the machine already understanding:

  • yarn characteristics

  • fabric behavior

  • shaping

  • stitch construction

  • what makes a garment feel modern

Machine knitting isn’t a different world — it’s the same language with a different accent.

Once you understand how the machine wants to work, everything clicks.

Why machine-knit patterns often feel dated

Most existing machine patterns were designed decades ago, for:

  • bulkier yarns

  • boxier styles

  • limited patterning options

  • minimal shaping

The fashion world has moved on.
Machine pattern libraries… less so.

But that doesn’t limit you.

Because machine knitters have a unique strength hand knitters don’t talk about:

We can adapt almost ANY hand-knit design to the machine — with simple math.

You are not stuck with:

  • drop shoulders

  • giant sleeves

  • stiff fits

  • or the “big hair” era aesthetic

You can knit exactly the silhouettes and styles you’re drawn to.

Hybrid Knitting: your secret weapon

One of the best advantages you have as a hand knitter using a machine is hybrid knitting.

Think of it this way:

Do the fun, expressive stitchwork by hand.
Let the machine handle the long, boring parts.

Examples:

  • knit the sweater body on the machine

  • add a hand-knit cable panel

  • finish the neckline or cuffs by hand

  • work texture where it matters and speed where it doesn’t

This approach creates modern, designer-level garments without the hours of hand knitting.

Yes, the machine has limits — but none that stop modern design

There are constraints:

  • Purl-heavy stitches require manual effort

  • Lace is possible, but easier on metal-bed patterning machines

  • Very wide pieces need paneling because of needlebed limits

But none of these prevent you from making current, beautiful, wearable garments.

In fact, once you understand how to “translate” a design, you gain creative freedom.

The fun part: translating your inspiration

If you’ve ever seen a sweater on Ravelry, Pinterest, or Instagram and thought:

“I wish I could make that on my machine…”

You can.

The process goes like this:

  1. Identify the silhouette

  2. Examine the stitch pattern

  3. Check what the machine can do easily

  4. Swap textures if needed

  5. Do the gauge math

  6. Build your plan

It’s surprisingly approachable once someone shows you how — and that’s exactly what I love helping knitters do.

If you have a pattern or inspiration image you’re excited about, send it to me.
I’d love to walk through it with you.

Coming soon: A modern approach to machine knitting

I’m working on a resource specifically for knitters who want to:

  • adapt hand-knit patterns to their machine

  • understand what translates well

  • build modern silhouettes

  • combine hand + machine knitting strategically

  • gain confidence in shaping, math, and planning

  • escape the “80s pattern look” forever

This may become a workshop… or even a signature Knit by Machine course.
If this resonates with you, keep an eye out — I’d love to help you build modern garments with clarity and confidence.
